blocks.text: “I declare,” he says, “I solemnly declare this. Until this crime is discovered and punished by the law, I almost feel as if there were a stain on my name. This gentleman gave a large part of his life to me. He gave the last day of his life to me. He often sat at my table and slept under my roof. He went from my house to his own, and he was struck down within an hour of leaving my house. I cannot say that he was not followed from my house. He may have been watched at my house. He may even have been chosen in the first place because of his connection with my house. That connection may have made people think he was richer than he was. It may have made him seem much more important than his own quiet, modest manner suggested. I have money, influence and a high position. If I cannot use them to bring into the light everyone who took part in such a crime, I will fail. I will fail to show my respect for that gentleman's memory. And I will fail to stay loyal to a man who was always loyal to me.”

He makes this protest with great emotion and seriousness. As he speaks, he looks round the room as if he were speaking to a large meeting. Mr. Bucket glances at him with a serious, watchful look. It would be a very bold thought. But there might be a touch of pity in that look.

“Today's ceremony,” Sir Leicester continues, “showed very clearly how much my dead friend was respected by the finest people in the land.” He puts weight on the word ‘friend’, because death makes all people equal. “This ceremony, I say, has made the shock of this most horrible and daring crime even worse for me. If my own brother had done it, I would not spare him.”
Mr. Bucket looks very serious. Volumnia says that the dead man was the most trustworthy and dearest person!
“You must feel it as a great loss, miss,” Mr. Bucket replies in a soothing voice. “No doubt. He was just the kind of man to be a loss. I'm sure he was.”

In reply, Volumnia lets Mr. Bucket understand several things. Her sensitive mind has firmly decided never to get over it as long as she lives. Her nerves are broken for ever. She does not have the least hope of smiling again. Meanwhile, she folds up a note in the shape of a cocked hat, a three-cornered hat. It is for that much-feared old general at Bath, and it describes her sad condition.
“It gives a delicate female a shock,” says Mr. Bucket kindly, “but it'll wear off.”

More than anything, Volumnia wants to know what is being done. Are they going to convict that dreadful soldier, or whatever it is they do? Did he have any accomplices, or whatever the thing is called in the law? She asks a great deal more of the same simple, innocent kind.

“Why, you see, miss,” Mr. Bucket answers. He uses his finger to help persuade her. He is so naturally polite to ladies that he almost said ‘my dear’. “It ain't easy to answer those questions at the present moment. Not at the present moment. I've kept myself on this case, Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet,”—Mr. Bucket brings Sir Leicester into the conversation because he is so important—“morning, noon, and night. If I hadn't had a glass or two of sherry, I don't think I could have kept my mind working so hard. I could answer your questions, miss, but my duty does not allow it. Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, will very soon be told everything that has been found out. And I hope that he may find it”—Mr. Bucket looks serious again—“to his satisfaction.”

The weak, feeble cousin only hopes some fellow will be hanged—as an example. Thinks it takes more influence to get a man hanged these days than to get a man a post worth ten thousand a year. Hasn't a doubt—as an example—far better to hang the wrong fellow than no fellow.
